method: Rate-vs-rate. Buy side = still-open lots bought since 2026-07-27 (lots.json, the only source with quantities -- trades.json has qty_diff populated only for 08-12). Sell side = the 31 scored stop fills in stops_analysis.json. Pro-rata attribution is NOT an independent check: it reduces algebraically to the same expression.
caveats: SURVIVORSHIP BIAS, upward, and it is the material one: lots.json retains only lots NOT yet FIFO-consumed, so any in-window buy that was itself later stopped out has been REMOVED from the buy side. Those are disproportionately losers (they got stopped). The +6.97% redeployment return is therefore flattered, and the true net is somewhat worse than -$31.47.

A third bucket is captured by NEITHER number: realised round-trip losses on churn. Example, NBIS 2026-08-06 -- bought 3sh @ $199.99 and stopped 3sh @ $190.87 two hours 24 minutes later, -4.56% on ~$601. The buy lot is gone from lots.json and the stop's own impact measures forward from the fill, not the round trip. Quantifying this fully needs a lot-level round-trip reconstruction.
Windows are similar but not matched: stop fills are 1-17 days old (median 7), buy lots 1-16 days.
Everything is priced at Wed 2026-08-12's close, an unusually strong session (SMH +2.08%, memory +5-9%). That inflates the foregone-upside side AND the redeployment side, partly self-cancelling.

GOOG lot (8.441 @ $325.79, $2,750) EXCLUDED -- lots.json still carries it though the position was closed the same day it was opened (swapped to GOOGL, which is also no longer held). A stale lot for a closed position is a data-integrity issue in its own right.
In-window buying ($33,392) exceeds stop proceeds ($28,242) by $5,150, funded by deposits and non-stop sells.
